question.problem:
Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}].$ *Hint: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $-1\pm 2\text{i}.$*
${e}^{At}={e}^{-t}\,\,$ {{field-1}} $2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)$
$-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)$ {{field-2}}
question.worked_solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 4{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -2{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues or $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=(-1+2\text{i})t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=(-1-2\text{i})t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((-1+2\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(-1+2\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(-1+2\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & ={e}^{-t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\ (-{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0})+2{\alpha }_{1}\text{i}t & ={e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\,{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}-{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ 2t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{1}{2t}{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-3{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-3\cdot \frac{1}{2t}{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot t+{e}^{-t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\  & ={e}^{-t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\ {\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{1}{2t}{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot t+{e}^{-t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\  & ={e}^{-t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].
$$
